name: Midland ER310 E+Ready Emergency Crank Weather Radio
summary: The most complete emergency radio here: real alerts, long runtime, and an AA backup for when every other source is gone.
verdict: The ER310 is the radio we would put in a household storm kit first. It covers AM, FM and NOAA weather radio, and with the weather alert switched on it sounds a siren when a warning is broadcast on your local channel. It can be powered four ways: its rechargeable lithium-ion pack, the hand crank, the solar panel, and six AA batteries as a backup. That AA option is the feature that sets it apart, because store-bought batteries are the one power source that works on day ten with no sun. Midland rates it for up to 45 hours of normal use. Midland’s own product page lists the battery as 3,500mAh in its features and 2,600mAh in its FAQ, so treat the exact capacity as unsettled. Midland is also refreshingly honest: its FAQ says the radio will not reliably charge newer iPhones and Android phones, that phone charging is for emergencies, and that solar alone will not revive a dead battery. Buy it for alerts, light and radio, which it does very well. Check today’s price and confirm stock, since Midland’s own store has listed it as out of stock at times.

name: Eton American Red Cross FRX3+ Weather Alert Radio
summary: A smaller, lighter alert radio with a battery backup, ideal for a go-bag or a second room.
verdict: The FRX3+ is the Red Cross-licensed radio from Eton, and it packs the important features into a smaller body than the Midland ER310. It receives all seven NOAA weather bands with an alert function, plus AM and FM. It runs on an internal lithium pack, which Eton’s manual lists as 2,600mAh at 3.7V, and it can be recharged by hand crank, by the small solar panel on top, or over USB. A AAA battery compartment gives you a backup that does not depend on the internal pack at all. For outage use, the light is well thought out: an LED flashlight, a red flashing beacon for signaling, and a glow-in-the-dark locator so you can find the radio in a dark room. Retail listings put it at about 15 oz, which makes it a sensible go-bag radio. The honest caveats: its solar panel is small, and reviewers note that solar charging is slower than on some competitors; and a 2,600mAh pack can only give a phone a partial top-up. Some retailers have listed the FRX3+ as no longer available, so check today’s price and stock on Amazon before you count on it.

name: Midland ER210 E+Ready Compact Emergency Crank Weather Radio
summary: The ER310’s little brother: same alert, smaller body, but no disposable-battery backup.
verdict: The ER210 takes the core of the ER310 and shrinks it. You still get AM, FM and NOAA weather radio with an automatic alert that sounds when a warning is issued on your local channel; Midland says the siren runs for eight seconds and can be silenced by holding the weather button. Power comes from a rechargeable lithium-ion pack, which Midland’s key features list as 2,600mAh, and it can be recharged by crank, by solar or over USB. Midland rates it for up to 25 hours of normal use. The flashlight is a Cree LED rated at 130 lumens with an SOS beacon, which is bright enough to move around a dark house. At 6.5 by 2.8 by 1.9 inches, it fits in a glovebox. What you give up compared with the ER310 is the AA backup, and that matters for long outages: once the internal pack is empty, you are cranking or waiting for sun. Midland’s FAQ is candid that solar extends the charge but does not fully charge the radio, and that many newer iPhones and Android phones may not charge from it. Check today’s price, as Midland often discounts the ER210 alongside the ER310.

name: Kaito KA500 Voyager Solar/Crank AM/FM/SW/NOAA Weather Alert Radio
summary: The radio for people who want shortwave and a proper reading lamp, and do not mind the size.
verdict: The Kaito KA500 Voyager is the most radio in this roundup. Alongside AM, FM and seven NOAA weather channels with an alert mode, it adds two shortwave bands, which listings give as roughly 3.2 to 8 MHz and 9 to 22 MHz. Shortwave is a niche feature most households will never use, but it is the one way to hear distant broadcasters if a regional disaster takes local stations off the air. Power options are the most flexible here: hand crank, a solar panel that tilts to face the sun, USB, an AC adapter and three AA batteries. Tilting matters, because a panel aimed at the sun produces noticeably more than one lying flat, a point our solar power bank guide makes about folding panels too. On the back of the panel is a 5-LED reading lamp, which is a better room light than a pinpoint flashlight. The drawbacks are size and variant confusion. Retail listings put it at about 1.8 lb and 8 by 5 by 2.5 inches. Battery specs differ by version: listings describe a small Ni-MH pack in the standard model, and some variants add a larger lithium pack or a dedicated phone charger. Check the exact listing and today’s price before buying.

name: RunningSnail MD-090P Emergency Crank Weather Radio
summary: A good outage radio and phone top-up battery, but not a warning device, because it does not list an alert.
verdict: The MD-090P is the pick for people who want the biggest battery in a crank radio and will rely on other sources for weather warnings. RunningSnail’s manual lists a 4,000mAh rechargeable battery, the largest here, and some retail listings express it as 14,800mWh, which is roughly the same pack described in energy rather than charge. It receives AM, FM and all seven NOAA weather channels, so you can listen to the forecast whenever you like. It can be recharged by crank, solar or USB. The light is a nice touch: a flashlight for walking and a reading lamp with a motion sensor that comes on when you pass in the dark, provided the switch is set to auto. The important limitation is that we could not find an automatic NOAA alert function listed for this model. That means it will not wake you for a tornado warning at 3 a.m. the way the Midland or Eton radios will. If you already have a weather alert radio or alerts on your phone, that is fine; if this is your only warning device, buy an alert radio instead. Check today’s price, as RunningSnail sells several similar models.

name: FosPower A1 Emergency Weather Radio (FOSPWB-2376)
summary: A sensible spare radio for a car or second kit, as long as something else handles weather alerts.
verdict: The FosPower A1 is the radio to buy when you want crank and solar backup in a car kit or a second go-bag and do not want to spend Midland money. Retail listings describe a 2,000mAh (7,400mWh) lithium-ion pack, recharged by hand crank, solar panel or micro-USB, plus a AAA battery compartment for backup. It receives AM, FM and the NOAA weather band from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz, so you can tune in to forecasts and emergency broadcasts. The flashlight is a modest 1W LED, and the IPX3 rating means it can handle splashes and light rain. What it does not list is an automatic weather alert, so like the RunningSnail it is a radio you listen to, not one that wakes you up. The small pack also limits its value as a phone charger; one owner review put it plainly, saying the crank is not enough to recharge other electronics, which matches what every maker in this category says in its own documentation. Charge the internal battery before storm season and keep spare AAAs with it. Check today’s price, as FosPower sells several similar models with different battery sizes, and confirm the model number.
